summary: The Gemara resolves whether R. Yehuda disputes the tevul yom ruling, derives that a tevul yom is valid for parah sprinkling, then transitions to Mishna chapter 5: the High Priest slaughters his bull, receives its blood in a bowl given to a kohen to stir, and prepares to enter the Holy of Holies with the golden firepan and incense ladle.

display.whats: Does R. Yehuda agree with the Mishna's ruling about the tevul yom's validity for the parah rite?
display.hint: Abaye explains that Ulla's principle (some verse-implications preclude earlier ones, some add on) means R. Yehuda actually does disagree - his silence in the Mishna does not mean consent.
display.title: Does R. Yehuda Disagree? Reading Silence in the Mishna

learning.ahaMoment: Silence in a Mishna is sometimes read as agreement - but here, given the logical structure of the verse conditions, Abaye argues R. Yehuda's silence is not agreement but omission.
learning.memoryAnchor: Ulla's principle: in legal verses, sometimes the conditions in a later clause cancel the earlier clause's conditions; sometimes they stack. The difference determines whether R. Yehuda disagrees.
learning.learnerQuestion: Does R. Yehuda actually disagree with the Mishna's ruling that a tevul yom is valid for the parah rite, even though he says nothing about it there?
learning.coreTension: R. Yehuda's silence in the Mishna could be read as agreement with the ruling that a tevul yom may sprinkle the parah waters, but Abaye argues that silence does not always signal consent.
learning.coreMove: Abaye applies Ulla's principle, that some implied verse-conditions preclude earlier ones while others stack onto them, to show the logical structure requires that R. Yehuda in fact disagrees, even though the Mishna records no explicit dissent from him.

takeaway.text: A scholar's silence in a Mishna does not automatically mean agreement; here, Ulla's principle about how implied verse-conditions interact shows that R. Yehuda's omission reflects a real, unstated disagreement rather than consent.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners often read a sage's silence in a Mishna as implicit agreement, missing that Abaye shows R. Yehuda's silence here actually conceals a real disagreement.

display.whats: How does the High Priest handle the bull's blood, and what are the laws of the incense offering inside the Holy of Holies?
display.hint: The Mishna describes the bull slaughter and blood-in-bowl sequence, then pivots to the incense offering - the most private act of Yom Kippur. The central dispute: must the incense be placed on the coals inside, or may it be prepared outside?
display.title: Bull's Blood, Golden Firepan, and the Pharisee-Sadducee Incense Dispute

learning.ahaMoment: The Sadducees wanted to prepare the incense cloud outside and walk in protected; the Sages said no - the act of placing incense on coals must happen inside, making the High Priest momentarily in danger before the cloud forms.
learning.memoryAnchor: The blood bowl is held by a kohen outside while the High Priest enters alone with fire and incense - the sequence requires him to be completely unaccompanied for the most sacred moment of the year.
learning.learnerQuestion: How does the High Priest handle the bull's blood, and where must the Yom Kippur incense actually be placed on burning coals: inside or outside the Holy of Holies?
learning.coreTension: The Sadducees held the incense should be prepared and lit outside so the High Priest enters already shielded by smoke, while the Sages insist the incense must be placed on the coals only after he is already inside the Holy of Holies, alone.
learning.coreMove: The Sages rule that the act of placing incense on coals must happen inside the Kodesh Kodashim itself, rejecting the Sadducee practice of pre-lighting outside, because the incense placement is a halakhic requirement of the rite rather than a means of physically shielding the High Priest.

takeaway.text: The bull's blood must be stirred continuously by a designated kohen so it does not congeal, and the incense must be placed on the coals inside the Holy of Holies, not prepared and carried in already burning, as the Sadducees held.

learning.learningBlocker: Learners may assume, with the Sadducee position, that the incense cloud functions as protective cover for the High Priest, missing that the Sages treat its inside-placement as a halakhic requirement of the rite, not a safety measure.

misconceptions.misconception: The incense cloud's purpose is to shield the High Priest from the danger of seeing the ark directly, so it should be prepared before he enters.
misconceptions.correction: The Sages hold the incense cloud is not a protective shield - placing the incense on the coals is a halakhic requirement of the rite itself, which is why it must happen only after the High Priest is already inside, not prepared beforehand as the Sadducees held.

rashiTranslations.en: Rashi: opens - since [the Gemara] said [that the statute applies] - [for] you cannot say [that the law applies] in this [case, because the whole passage teaches].

Rashi: continues - by implication [it] is [understood] - and by necessity they disagree - and [the] pure [one shall] sprinkle - this [word] 'pure' is extra, [it] was not [necessary to write it, except to teach].

Rashi: continues - from the implication [of the whole] [passage] it must be [that he is] impure - [for the verse says] 'and [the] pure one shall sprinkle on the impure' - [by] implication he [becomes] impure.
Rashi: continues - [the Gemara says:] when they examined [the] tradition closely - [they] did not accept [this derivation] from [the verse].

Rashi: continues - [meaning] they could not establish it [firmly by means of logical] argument [drawn] from [the] tradition - so as to [be able] to grasp [the full extent of the law by] its [textual basis].
Rashi: continues - [so] that all their [textual] derivations [would be] bringing [forth] this [meaning].
Rashi: continues - [either] immediately this [with] that - or all of them [are] established this after [that].
Rashi: continues - [by the reasoning of] how [much the] more [is this true], as [it is] established [in the teaching] of [the] Rabbi [from the Academy] - [the Gemara brings a] parallel [case].
Rashi: continues - [the analogy is:] just as the fox [goes] on [its] legs when [it] treads [the] field.
Rashi: continues - [the] measure of [the] law gives - [meaning it is fitting and proper to establish the law].
Rashi: continues - [the meaning is:] thus [it is fitting] to say [that] after he confessed [his sin] upon himself, he will [become] innocent, [and therefore will be] fit to atone [for] others.
Rashi: continues - [the Mishna states:] for anyone who was treading [in] it - [he must wait until the] incense service [is performed].
Rashi: continues - [the teaching is about one who was] treading [in the courtyard] - [the Gemara explains:] it was trampled in it [by] the feet [of the treaders].
Rashi: continues - [so] that [they should] not [become] crumbly - [this must happen] when they wait [until the time].
Rashi: continues - until the incense service [is performed] - as [is] arranged in the [Torah] portion.
Rashi: continues - [the Mishna discusses] on the fourth row [of the] Temple floor - [the] entire floor was made [of] rows [and] rows of [stone] tablets - stones of marble.
Rashi: continues - and each row [was] called a row [or] row of tablets - and [the Gemara] was wondering [whether the rule applies].
Rashi: continues - [to] the fourth row [of stones] - [each] row [and] row was made of [different] types of marble stones - [and every line].
Rashi: continues - [was] and each row is called a row [course] - and [the Gemara mentions:] it was wondering.
Rashi: continues - [about] whether [it is on] the fourth row [where] from the entrance of the Temple [building], and inside [the Temple, Rashi notes that the discussion concerns the placement].
Rashi: continues - [regarding the] incense [service] - [the Mishna continues:] [the High Priest took] a censer - [a vessel containing hot] coals.

Rashi: continues - [he] left them [the coals] until the incense [will be] burned [from the coals] - and [he] gave [them] into the [incense] pan - and afterward he [will] bring [both] the pan and the censer inside.

Rashi: continues - [the Gemara asks about] each day - [when] the [High Priest] takes coals from the second arrangement of incense [to] bring [them to] the inner altar for the incense [of] morning and evening.

Rashi: continues - [continuing with the rules about] coals - [the description of how they are taken] from [the] second arrangement [of the] incense to put [them] on the inner altar for incense [of] morning and evening.
Rashi: continues - [the High Priest] takes [the coals] - [one] who takes coals from [the] second arrangement of the incense to bring [them to the altar for the daily] incense [services].

Rashi: continues - [continuing the description of the coals used] on this day [Yom Kippur] - [the coals are] broad [in size] - [because on Yom Kippur the procedure differs] from [the regular daily procedure].
Rashi: continues - [the Mishna states:] the censer [of] silver - [the Gemara] explains the reason [for the specific material used].
Rashi: continues - and this day [Yom Kippur the censer] is broad - [the Gemara notes:] the reason for Yom Kippur [being different is].
Rashi: continues - because of [the High Priest's] weakness [of body, as] the High Priest [on Yom Kippur must maintain] strength [for all the] services.
Rashi: continues - and this day [Yom Kippur the censer] is long [extended] - [this] is [so] that [the High Priest] may place his hand [well] below [his] arm [for leverage].
Rashi: continues - and his arm [will be] [a] support [to him] - [the Mishna continues with other measurements, such as:] a handful - [of incense].
Rashi: continues - [equivalent to] half a mana - [the High Priest also] added [to it] a full [handful for an] additional offering.
Rashi: continues - [explaining that the portions are:] he [the High Priest] brings [into] the Holy [of] Holies alone [only] a handful of the incense [but there is an additional portion].
Rashi: continues - [of] the morning and of the evening [incense, which are placed] on the inner altar - [in these portions the High Priest adds the extra handful].
Rashi: continues - and this day [Yom Kippur the incense is] fine - [made from] the finest [particles] - [the Mishna states that the incense is more finely ground].

Rashi: continues - [explaining:] just as [when] he [would] bring [incense into the Holy of] Holies, he would return [it the next day] - [the next morning, before] evening [Yom Kippur, to the mortar [and he would grind [it very].
Rashi: continues - fine - [the Mishna explains the measure of fineness required on that day].
Rashi: continues - [continuing the Mishna's discussion:] each day the priests [who are] going up to the altar [are described] - [the Mishna specifies how the priests ascend].

Rashi: continues - [they are] going up by the edge of the eastern [side] of the ramp - [because] the east [side of the ramp] is [designated] for [one who is going] to the right [of the one ascending].
Rashi: continues - since his face [is] to [the] north [when he is on the ramp, because the] ramp [is in the] south [of the altar, and the one].
Rashi: continues - [when he is] going up [on] the ramp - [since] he [is going up] in the south [direction, and because].
Rashi: continues - all the beginning of [all] its corners [are] to the right [according to the direction he faces, it] is not [fitting] [that].

Rashi: continues - he [should be] circling [the altar] not for [the sake of the] service - and the width of the ramp [is] sixteen cubits - [the High Priest] goes up [via the] east [side] and [he] circles the altar for his [priestly] service.
Rashi: continues - and [he] descends to the [side of the] left [which is the] edge of the west [side] - [the Mishna continues with] and this day [Yom Kippur, when the High Priest is serving].

Rashi: continues - [the] High Priest [is treating himself with special care] - [he shows] the glory and the affection of [the people of] Israel, [since] he [is] their messenger - and [he] makes himself [appear] like a son of the house - and if he came.

Rashi: continues - to go up to the altar for the [priestly] service - [such as] for the giving of blood of the daily [offerings] and [the] additions - [and the male goat of the people circles the entire ramp] for [the sake of] service and not for [the sake of the] service.

Rashi: continues - [the High Priest demonstrates] his honor and the affection of [the nation of] Israel [since he is their representative] - [he] does [this to show that] he [himself] [is] a son of [the Temple] house - and if [it] came.

Rashi: continues - [that the High Priest came] to go up to the altar [to perform] service - [such as] for the giving of blood [of the offering] of the daily [sacrifices] and [the additional offerings].
Rashi: continues - [and in contrast, the] male goat of the [common] people [circles the entire ramp] for [the sake of the] service - and not [only] for [the sake of the] service [alone].
Rashi: continues - [the Mishna states:] four arrangements [of wood]... [the Gemara] explains [this in detail].
Rashi: concludes - [this begins the discussion that will continue into the next section].
Rashi: continues - Gemara: and [is it] not written 'and [every] man' [in the verse]? - and [the Gemara] establishes [that].

Rashi: continues - it [the verse] is [speaking] below [in another context], at the time of the incense [service] - and [so when the Mishna] says 'it is trampled in him on the fourth row of [the Temple building]'.

Rashi: continues - [this is about the time] when [one] leaves the Temple [building] to the [outer] courtyard - [one must] count the rows [of stone] - and this [arrangement is called the] fourth [row] of the Temple [building].

Rashi: continues - [the] Mishna [of] the Temple [building discusses] 'when [one] leaves [the] Temple [building] to the [outer] courtyard [and] counts the rows - and this [is] the fourth [row] for the Temple [building].'
Rashi: continues - [the Tanna] taught [that this is called] 'of the Temple' - [meaning the] fourth row [specifically] of the Temple [building, not of the] courtyard.
Rashi: continues - [continuing the discussion:] when he leaves the Temple [building] to the [outer] courtyard - [he] counts the rows - [to determine if it is the fourth row].
Rashi: continues - and this [is the] fourth [row] for the Temple [building].
Rashi: concludes - [end of this section of detailed discussion on the Temple structure and Yom Kippur procedures].
